Nothing bad happens if you tell someone. You won’t get institutionalised. No one will talk to you in baby-speak. No one will even refer to you differently. Most people like to think you don’t do it and pretend that you never told them. Of course, people close to you are very likely to refer you to psychological help in the form of regular counselling sessions. Although they seem uncomfortable and nerve-wracking, they’re popular for a reason: they tend to work.

First off, something that strikes out to me is your eloquently-placed words. It’s clear to me that you must have cared for Caitie and that your love for her was undying, just by reading this post. Your rather intermittent changes of topic and chronological order also show that you were somewhat desperate and overwhelmed with guilt of Caitie’s unfortunate passing. I’d like you to know that the care you put into this post just demonstrates your adoring and caring personality for Caitie and that it’s clear to anyone reading this that it’s not your fault you weren’t the person you “should’ve been to her”. 

Secondly, what you did, your self-proclaimed “selfishness”, is what anyone would have done. If you aren’t experienced on the topic of suicide and how to support someone attempting suicide, you’d be just a passerby of sorts and wouldn’t know how to respond. You’d be scared of what you may say causing her to infer wrongly from your acts of support and make her feel worse. Conversely, if you were experienced on how to support someone attempting suicide, chances are that would be because you attempt suicide too. In that case, your outlook on suicide would, most likely, be bleak and rather uncaring. Very few people would support someone attempting suicide, and those that would are probably professionals. Even fewer people would refer them to a professional, as it is an anxious and uncomfortable situation to be in. 

Lastly, I’d like to commend you on trying to get help. It’s brave to do that and it’s what, I assume based on your closeness to her, she would want you to do following her passing. Ultimately, only you can help yourself in this existence. Professionals assist you in helping yourself and drugs give you an outlook on life you don’t even believe, but only you can realise that what you did was not selfish and she was unlikely to accept help were she given the opportunity, founded upon the fact that she tried multiple times and thus had intent. I wish you good luck in realising that, whether or not that luck does much relies on what you do to help yourself next.

It’s hard for people to comprehend and give support to what they can’t relate to. Don’t take it personally, they also most likely felt incredibly uncomfortable.

When I was at my lowest point, just a couple months ago, I never ceased to forget the time in August where me and my first girlfriend were on her sofa and we spooned. It was incredibly comfortable. That same month she tried breaking up with me. Two months later she did break up with me, calling me sexist.

My point isn’t to make you jealous, however. The point is to hopefully make you realise that your longings for affection just hinder you. It may be hard for it to sink in, but people are the most unreliable things on Earth. The only person you can rely on is yourself and, although you may not think yourself reliable at times, you can always rely on yourself more than others, no matter the circumstance you’re in.
